lesson_title: The Earth Is a Peach: Inside Our Planet
hook_text: The deepest hole humans ever drilled barely scratched the planet. So how do we know what's at the centre?
clip_script: Bite a peach down to the stone and you are holding a scale model of the earth. The skin is the crust — feel how thin it is, and that is honestly generous: five to seventy kilometres deep, on a planet six thousand three hundred and seventy-one kilometres to the middle. Every city, every farm, every mine sits in that skin. The flesh is the mantle, and just like the peach it is most of the fruit — about eighty-four per cent of the planet. And here is what everyone gets wrong: it is NOT liquid. It is solid rock. One band near the top is simply soft, like a slab of chocolate left in the cubbyhole on a summer drive — still a solid bar, but leave it leaning and it slowly slumps. That slumping band is why the continents can drift. The stone is the core: liquid iron stirring on the outside — the whole reason a compass needle knows where north is — and a solid iron ball at the centre, five to six thousand degrees, as hot as the surface of the sun. Why does the hottest spot not melt? The weight of the entire earth is pressing on it. When heat and pressure argue, pressure wins.
visual_style: A bitten peach morphing into a cutaway planet, labels appearing on skin, flesh and stone; chocolate slumping in a hot car; a compass needle steadying as liquid metal swirls.
mood: Lunchbox science — a whole planet hiding in one piece of fruit.
pacing: Easy through the three parts, sharpening on the two myths, closing hard on 'pressure wins'.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to hear how missing earthquake waves proved the core is liquid.
